name: Sodium hyaluronate
lead: Sodium hyaluronate is the sodium salt of hyaluronic acid (HA), a linear polysaccharide of repeating glucuronic acid and N-acetylglucosamine units found in skin, joint fluid and the eye [1][2]. It is the form usually listed in moisturisers and serums, and it is also used in medical products such as joint injections and ophthalmic surgical viscoelastics.

In skincare it is described as a humectant that binds water; lower-molecular-weight versions are marketed as penetrating deeper [1]. Evidence cited for sodium hyaluronate in the medical literature comes mainly from injectable or surgical uses rather than cosmetic topicals.
infobox: Hyalgan, Supartz, Euflexxa, Monovisc, Orthovisc, Healon

paras: Sodium hyaluronate is added to creams and serums for hydration and is said by manufacturers to improve elasticity [1]. Cross-linked HA is also used in injectable dermal fillers, with effects lasting roughly 6 to 12 months [3].

Sodium hyaluronate products are used for knee osteoarthritis injections [4][5], as viscoelastic agents in cataract surgery [6][7], and as a submucosal lift in endoscopic resection [8][9]. Studies have also examined a sodium hyaluronate membrane for preventing postoperative abdominal adhesions [10].

With fillers, reported complications include pain, bruising, redness, itching, vascular occlusion and nerve or microvessel injury, and occasional granulomatous reactions [3]. A Grokipedia summary states hypersensitivity and infection are rare [1]. Topical use is generally described as well tolerated, though irritation and allergy are possible with any cosmetic ingredient.

Hyaluronic acid was isolated by Karl Meyer and John Palmer in 1934 [3]. Pharmacia developed the ophthalmic product Healon in the 1970s and 1980s [3]. A 1985 Science paper reported that HA degradation products induced angiogenesis [11], and a 1985 study measured sodium hyaluronate concentration and molecular weight in synovial fluid across arthropathies [12].

Most trials involve medical rather than cosmetic uses. A 1998 randomized trial of intra-articular sodium hyaluronate (Hyalgan) in knee osteoarthritis was reported by the Hyalgan Study Group [4], and a registered trial with 421 participants compared two brands for knee OA [5]. Registered trials also cover shoulder, ankle and hip osteoarthritis [13][14][15], tennis elbow [16], and cataract surgery viscoelastics [6][7]. A 2010 Lancet systematic review examined injections including hyaluronate for tendinopathy [17]. No trial of topical sodium hyaluronate for facial appearance was found in this source set.

card.summary: The salt form of hyaluronic acid in most moisturisers and serums; well established medically, with little direct data on topical looks effects.
card.note: Strong evidence base is for injections and surgery, not facial creams.

quick.overview:
Sodium hyaluronate is the common salt form of hyaluronic acid, a water-binding molecule naturally present in skin and joints. It appears in many moisturisers and serums.

Most clinical research concerns joint injections and eye surgery rather than cosmetic creams.
quick.mechanism: It is a humectant that binds water; lower-molecular-weight versions are marketed as penetrating deeper.
quick.risks: Topical use is generally described as well tolerated. Injectable forms (fillers) carry reported risks such as bruising, vascular occlusion and granulomas.
